title: Doppler shift from a moving source

questions.prompt: State what is meant by the Doppler effect.
A progressive sound wave keeps the same shape but its amplitude becomes twice as large. What happens to its intensity?

options.C: It becomes four times as large.

questions.prompt: A sound source moves directly towards a stationary observer in still air. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The wavefront spacing at the observer is smaller and the observed frequency is higher.
options.B: The wavefront spacing is smaller and the observed frequency is lower.
options.C: The wavefront spacing is larger and the observed frequency is higher.
options.D: The wavefront spacing and observed frequency are unchanged.

questions.prompt: A sound source moves away from a stationary observer. Which quantity remains unchanged because the air is stationary and its conditions are constant?

options.C: The speed of sound through the air
options.D: The number of wavefronts arriving each second

questions.prompt: A cyclist rings a bell continuously while riding directly past a person who is standing still.

parts.prompt: Explain why the person detects a higher frequency while the cyclist approaches.
Explain the change in observed frequency after the cyclist has passed and is moving away.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows four successive positions S1 to S4 of a sound source moving to the right. A stationary observer P is to the right of S4 and a stationary observer Q is to the left of S1.

figure.purpose: Assess construction and interpretation of moving-source wavefront geometry without revealing the result.
figure.brief: Original Cambridge-inspired black-and-white line diagram. Horizontal source path with S1, S2, S3, S4 equally spaced left to right, motion arrow right, observer Q left and P right. Provide empty space for the learner to draw wavefront arcs. Do not show wavefronts or frequency labels.
figure.alt_text: Four successive source positions lie between stationary observers Q on the left and P on the right.

parts.prompt: On the diagram, draw four wavefronts produced at S1, S2, S3 and S4 at equal time intervals.
Compare the wavefront spacing reaching P with that reaching Q.
Compare the frequencies detected by P and Q and explain your answer.

questions.prompt: A loudspeaker moves through still air at constant speed towards a stationary microphone. The sound speed is 330 m s$^{-1}$. The spacing of successive wavefronts in front of the loudspeaker is measured as 0.60 m. Behind the loudspeaker, the spacing is 0.75 m.

figure.purpose: Support a mixed wave-equation and Doppler comparison by making the two measured spacings spatially unambiguous.
figure.brief: Original Cambridge-inspired black-and-white line diagram with moving loudspeaker centred, microphone ahead, close straight wavefront markers labelled 0.60 m ahead and wider markers labelled 0.75 m behind. Show equal speed arrows on one front in each region. Do not display frequencies or calculations.
figure.alt_text: A moving loudspeaker has wavefront spacing 0.60 metres ahead and 0.75 metres behind.

parts.prompt: Use the wave equation to calculate the frequency of wavefronts arriving at the microphone.
Calculate the frequency that would be detected by a stationary microphone behind the loudspeaker.
Use your answers to explain why source motion changes observed frequency even though the speed of sound through the air is unchanged.
